items.q: A specific input used to check that a program works is a…
An unusual input that often breaks programs, like an empty maze, is an…

choices: what should happen vs what did happen

items.q: Your program passes grids A and B but fails grid C, which has no gems. What kind of test is C?
items.why: Grid C tests an unusual case the others miss: a grid with no gems. That is an edge case.

items.q: Which test would catch a loop count that is one too many?
choices: a wide open grid with no walls at all
a grid with extra gems to pick up
no test can catch a count bug
a grid where the goal is right before a wall
items.why: If the count is one too many, Bolt steps one square too far. A goal just before a wall makes that extra step fail loudly.

items.q: You fixed grid C but now grid A fails. What does systematic testing say?
choices: run all the test grids again after every fix
grid A does not matter once C passes
delete grid A from the tests
only test the newest grid, C
items.why: A fix can break something that used to pass. Running every test grid again proves nothing else broke.

items.q: A list of who does what by when is a…
Notes that help the next person understand a program are…
Your tester found level 2 confusing. Incorporating their feedback means…
choices: changing the level and testing again
blaming the tester for playing badly
items.why: Incorporating feedback means acting on it: change the level, then test again to see if it helped.

items.q: You have 18 minutes to build, test and fix a level. What helps most?
choices: set a time for each part before you start
build until the time runs out
keep changing the plan as you go
items.why: A simple plan with a time for each part keeps build, test and fix all covered before the minutes run out.

items.q: Which level note helps the next person most?
choices: "Level 3: the key is behind the water; you need if has key"
items.why: A helpful note points at the tricky part and the idea that solves it, so the next person is not stuck.
